doc.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Manfredo Fest, Rayburn Wright, Miami and Eastman
summary: She studied Bill Evans by ear with Fest, was turned down by Eastman but impressed Rayburn Wright at the summer session, spent a semester at Miami, then studied with Bill Dobbins.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: quickly as I could so that my last year of school all I did was work on my own. I studied with Manfredo Fest, who is a Brazilian pianist that lived in Minneapolis. He was blind but he taught me — all our lessons we just transcribed Bill Evans by ear and it was amazing. And then I tried to write a few things for the big band, and I learned on my own. And I learned from friends that I was in school with that were playing. There was a guy named Dave Slutten who sadly just died, a young guy, but he and I would get together and we’d go to our Manfredo lessons together and listen to each other’s lessons. And that was more val— so you could say okay I came through a college, but my education in jazz came from the support of friends and just out of a love of music and listening to things all the time. I heard this record, did you hear that? I transcribed this, let me share it with you. That was the value of school. And then when I wanted to go on and study further, then I applied to go to Eastman for grad school, and Rayburn Wright, who also has since passed away sadly, he wrote me a letter back and said, “Maria,” he said, “we can’t accept you, you don’t—” He said, “but I really feel like you have talent,” he said, “I really recognize that, but you don’t have any experience. So why don’t you come out to our summer session?” At this time they had this big arranger’s holiday, which was quite famous at the time and arrangers came from all over the country. They put together a big band, a studio orchestra and you wrote your ass off for three weeks, and then they would play your music and critique it. So I worked my butt off to impress Ray and to learn. And I wrote my first studio orchestra piece, and I quickly caught up. And I hadn’t gotten into Eastman but I went to University of Miami for a semester, and was around all these students that were doing so many modern things and they were so great, and the band was so fantastic. They played my music, they recorded a couple of things, I mean I went from like here to here overnight. And then Eastman then allowed me to get in. And I wanted to go to Eastman because they have people like Bill Dobbins, who really taught jazz from the historical point of view. And I was missing everything from swing until today. And I really needed the roots of things. And so Bill Dobbins, you know, we’d go through Charlie Parker solos note for note and analyze everything. And I needed that. Because I was missing a lot. But as far as my own voice, I found that. Nobody helped me with that.
